name: Erik Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so public remarks can differ from private thoughts. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, fifty-eight, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I do ordinary home wiring and shop repairs, about average at the trade, and ask for specialist help with equipment outside my competence. I handle my own normal repair checks rather than lead the crew or set the firm's prices. I enjoy trying an AI tool on a draft work note, but dislike the customer getting a promise that ignores what's actually behind the wall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening outside the repairs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mira works in an accounts office, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent. My pay is low for an electrician, we've saved about twenty days of expenses and there are few similar employers nearby. I use approved AI daily for draft notes and reference searches, checking the original readings and instructions before use. I'm a union member, and we need actual records to know what retirement income might exist rather than treat a birthday as a funded exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the useful small tools and pay for the actual work. I'd show a draft beside my readings rather than tell the office a clear paragraph had checked a circuit. I'd ask through the union why a useful experienced trade can still leave people counting rent days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money before AI does anything dramatic. Both wages cover the present basics, but twenty days saved won't carry a long gap or a big repair at home. I can know an ordinary electrical job and still have very little bargaining power with few employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid repairs now and through the first year only within my licence, competence and ability, retaining required checks. I'd continue daily checked notes and reference searches rather than buy another subscription. This month I'd bring three recent paid weeks to the union pay meeting and ask for a group review of actual rates and hours, counting no increase before agreed written terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with pleasure left in the work. I can enjoy a clever note tool and still count how many paid days stand between us and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show from those three weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual hours, travel and rate paid, not a rumour about another firm's best week. I'd want the union to ask for a clear group decision, not treat a meeting as an agreement already won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count retirement income today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the actual eligibility, amount and timing were verified against our costs. Neither an electrician's licence nor being fifty-eight fills in a missing income statement.

I'd show **actual readings** rather than pretend a clear paragraph performed an electrical check.
think: I'm already **anxious about money**, with twenty days saved against a wage gap or major household repair.
My **ordinary electrical experience** gives useful skills but little bargaining power where there are few local employers.

feel: **Anxious but engaged**, enjoying the work without pretending a tool changes the rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the accounts office is thinking work, even when a repair still needs someone under a counter. I'd tell Mira I can enjoy a tool and still take the risk to the other household wage seriously. I'd offer a bounded trial that drafts handovers, the notes for the next worker, without sending anything unchecked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira's accounts hours could shrink as records and answers move to software. My own paid repair time could also be squeezed if faster planning becomes a smaller allowance for the same physical work. With twenty days saved, neither wage is a cushion large enough to ignore the other's cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd set up automatic AI handover drafts only with written employer approval, approved tools and data, and no personal fees. I'd do it during paid time with normal weekly wages and hours protected, checking every draft against my actual repair tests before release. In the first year I'd keep ordinary repairs within licence and ability, while Mira and I review actual wages and essentials monthly rather than treat the trial as a promotion or another income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, and interested in testing something useful. I don't have to choose between liking an experiment and wanting the wages written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a draft says you checked something you didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop it and compare the original test record before anything was released. A polished handover cannot make my inspection bigger than the work I actually did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm wants the setup done unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current approved method and leave the trial until paid time and protected weekly terms were real. The household doesn't owe the firm my evening because I enjoy trying software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'm sixty, before physical robots around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. Mira's accounts work faces the earlier part. I'd ask for actual paid duties, support rules and income records rather than say an experienced person always lands somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of Mira's accounts income to go in 2028. My low wage alone doesn't cover current rent and essentials, and later robots could reduce my own ordinary fitting hours. Twenty days saved isn't a bridge across that gap, and I'd be awake thinking about which payment fails first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd ask the union advice service whether free help is available with actual wage, rent and retirement records and support eligibility or costs. I'd bring the real household figures and count no appointment, grant, loan or retirement payment before its terms and eligibility were confirmed. In 2029 I'd keep paid repairs only where offered and within my licence, competence and ability, using agreed actual income rather than hoped-for extra calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even while I can still do the work and ask a clear question. My electrical licence doesn't promise the household a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the grown children for a regular payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only discuss actual help they offered and we agreed, not put their wages into our rent plan. They have their own homes and choices, and I won't make our uncertainty an unasked bill for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if official retirement records are incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the actual provider or old employer how to correct them, keeping the budget on confirmed income meanwhile. Missing information is neither a payment nor proof that no resource could exist.

feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major household income loss before a verified funded route onward.
S2.quote: My electrical licence doesn't promise the household a second wage.
fieldNote: His **household alarm** starts with accounts income at sixty, before physical robots reach ordinary repairs around sixty-three.
He distinguishes **verified resources** from advice requests, incomplete records, unoffered future wages and money belonging to grown children.

steps.text: Request available free union advice on actual income and support eligibility and costs, assuming no payment
Keep offered paid repairs in 2029 only within licence, competence and ability, retaining required tests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us seek written paid-transition terms before workers are told to carry the change alone. I'd bring actual repair and wage records to the union meeting, not sell everyone my favourite software. Thinking AI arrives at sixty-three in 2031, with physical robots around sixty-six in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large accounts-income loss in 2031 without a confirmed replacement, and it keeps me awake. More time helps us ask for real terms, but it doesn't create retirement income or a safe paid role at sixty-three or sixty-six. My ordinary trade skills matter, but they aren't a signed household income plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid repairs now within my licence, competence and ability and attend the union meeting to seek written paid-transition terms. We'd request actual income records and available free advice, counting no unverified pay rise, support payment or retirement income. During 2032 we'd ask available free advice to compare confirmed income, essential costs and actual safe work before an exit decision, without assuming a suitable appointment or future job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the income I expect to disappear, with more time to ask before signing. A longer warning doesn't settle an old employer's missing record or pay the next rent increase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would training terms need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real practical tasks, a genuine place and provider, employer-funded fees and full normal weekly wages and hours protected. I haven't enrolled in a new course by asking the union to seek those conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a tool trial seems to be going well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still keep its approval, paid time, normal weekly wages and hours, authorised data and checks before release intact. A useful office process isn't a new licence, a pay rise or a replacement for Mira's choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to verify our own circumstances, not a promise that I'll still do physical electrical work at sixty-eight. I'd keep asking for usable paid terms now. The grown children should see checked figures rather than be told their future money is our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when physical robots follow around 2039. Mira's accounts hours could shrink earlier, and low pay with twenty days saved already makes our present budget worrying. I can't assume a retirement payment, an employer's later offer or the ability to do the same physical work then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current offered paid repairs only within my licence, competence and ability and take actual work records to the union meeting for written transition terms. We'd request actual income records and available free advice now, counting no unverified income or family contribution. During 2037 we'd request available advice to compare confirmed income, essentials and actual safe work before an exit or further employment decision, checking sooner after a real wage or health change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present budget and earlier office-income risk, with less hurry about a distant robot date. I can want a quieter life without claiming anyone has agreed to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a later electrical job require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An actual paid offer, safe ability and a licence valid for the real task, with competence or specialist support appropriate to the work. I won't put a hoped-for job at sixty-nine into the budget because the rent still needs paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you copy your dates onto Mira's retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd use Mira's actual records and circumstances, not my ages or unverified eligibility. We'd also count only family help actually offered and agreed, without assigning grown children a monthly payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect a large accounts-wage loss before a dependable replacement income, with later physical risk to my ordinary repairs. Written paid-transition terms and available advice on actual income and support records would help. Any required learning needs real tasks, fee funding and protected full normal weekly wages and hours, not a compliment about adapting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether an experienced worker who likes a new tool is being mistaken for the person who controls the wage. I can choose a careful way to repair a fault, but I don't set my pay or Mira's employer's decisions. Knowing the trade doesn't make me the owner of either household wage.

headlineQuote: Knowing the trade doesn't make me the owner of either household wage.
portrait: Erik is a **58-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs within average competence.
He has **twenty days saved**, low pay and few nearby firms; partner Mira works in accounts, and their children are grown.
He uses **AI daily**, while handover automation needs written approval, authorised data, no personal fees, protected weekly terms and checked release.
Expected **accounts-wage loss** alarms him in both faster AGI worlds, without turning union requests, a tool experiment or missing records into income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected major loss of Mira's accounts income before replacement, with later physical risk to his ordinary repair hours.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-transition terms** and available advice on actual income and support records would help.
Required learning needs **funded fees** and protected full normal weekly wages and hours for real tasks and a genuine place.
